qualification: NSSCO Economics 6145 (syllabus vNIED 2018; implementation 2019; first examination 2020, examined 2026)

items.prompt: Explain why an invented goods trade deficit widens when exports rise N$80m to N$100m and imports N$90m to N$120m.
items.canonical_answer: Export receipts rise N$20m but import payments rise N$30m. Goods trade therefore moves from −N$10m to −N$20m; export growth alone does not establish an improved trade balance.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): both flows rise. Because/mechanism (2): export increase N$20m (1), imports N$30m (1). Consequence (1): deficit widens N$10m to N$20m.
objective_titles: Describe the changing patterns of exports and imports and the effects on the balance of payments

items.prompt: Explain why a higher value of imported machinery need not mean greater current consumer spending on foreign goods.
items.canonical_answer: Machinery is productive equipment rather than household consumption. The composition of imports changes the interpretation even though both contribute to import payments.
marking_guidance: Context (1): imported equipment. Reason/conclusion (1): distinguish investment-related goods from consumer imports.
objective_titles: Describe the changing patterns of exports and imports and the effects on the balance of payments

items.prompt: Explain the error in treating a goods trade deficit as the whole balance of payments.
items.canonical_answer: Goods trade compares goods exports and imports. The balance of payments also includes services, income, transfers and financing, so the narrower balance cannot stand for the full account.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): goods subset treated as full account. Boundary/test (1): identify other external components.
objective_titles: Describe the changing patterns of exports and imports and the effects on the balance of payments

items.prompt: Explain why an overseas investor’s acquisition of a lasting ownership interest in a domestic workshop is not itself a current-account goods export.
items.canonical_answer: The ownership investment is a financial-account flow. A later sale of workshop output abroad would be a separate export of current goods.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): investment funding mistaken for export. Boundary/test (1): ownership transaction versus sale of output.
objective_titles: Describe the changing patterns of exports and imports and the effects on the balance of payments

items.prompt: Explain how stronger foreign demand for a currency can cause appreciation in a hypothetical floating economy, with currency supply and other relevant conditions unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: Foreign buyers need the currency for purchases or investment. Demand increases against unchanged supply, raising its price in other currencies. This hypothetical mechanism does not describe an independent Namibia dollar/rand movement under the maintained peg.
marking_guidance: Starting change (1): currency demand rises. Mechanism (2): purchases require currency (1), unchanged supply meets stronger demand (1). Consequence (1): appreciation under floating conditions.
objective_titles: Discuss exchange rates and give reasons for their fluctuations

items.prompt: Explain the import-cost effect of US$1 rising from N$18 to N$20 for a US$100 input, with the rand peg maintained and its dollar price unchanged.
items.canonical_answer: The Namibia dollar depreciates against the US dollar. The input rises from N$1,800 to N$2,000, a N$200 increase; there is no independent movement against the rand in this case.
marking_guidance: Context (1): third-currency quotation and fixed dollar price. Reason/consequence (1): N$200 dearer input under maintained peg.
objective_titles: Discuss exchange rates and give reasons for their fluctuations

items.prompt: Invented equal-resource one-period maxima: A 12 mats or 6 baskets; B 4 mats or 4 baskets. Constant opportunity costs, comparable goods, no transport costs. Calculate the opportunity cost of one basket for each producer.
items.canonical_answer: A sacrifices 12/6 = 2 mats per basket; B sacrifices 4/4 = 1 mat per basket.
marking_guidance: Formula/substitution (1): alternative mats divided by baskets. Result/units (1): A 2 and B 1 mat per basket.
objective_titles: Demonstrate the simple application of absolute and comparative advantage in trade

items.prompt: Invented equal-resource one-period maxima: A 12 mats or 6 baskets; B 4 mats or 4 baskets. Constant opportunity costs, comparable goods, no transport costs. Analyse the absolute and comparative advantages.
items.canonical_answer: A has absolute advantage in both goods. A’s mat costs half a basket versus B’s one, so A has comparative advantage in mats; B’s basket costs one mat versus A’s two, so B has comparative advantage in baskets.
marking_guidance: Pattern (1): A greater absolute output both. Evidence (1): 12/6 versus 4/4. Explanation (2): A lower mat cost (1), B lower basket cost (1).
objective_titles: Demonstrate the simple application of absolute and comparative advantage in trade

items.prompt: Invented equal-resource one-period maxima: A 12 mats or 6 baskets; B 4 mats or 4 baskets. Constant opportunity costs, comparable goods, no transport costs. Explain the error in concluding that B cannot gain from trade because A has absolute advantage in both goods.
items.canonical_answer: B has the lower opportunity cost of baskets, one mat rather than two. Trade between those opportunity costs can benefit both, despite A’s absolute output advantage.
marking_guidance: Confusion (1): absolute advantage substituted for comparative. Boundary/test (1): B lower basket opportunity cost permits mutual gain.
objective_titles: Demonstrate the simple application of absolute and comparative advantage in trade

items.canonical_answer: Producing more with the same resources, or the same output with fewer resources.
objective_titles: Describe absolute advantage

items.prompt: Invented equal-resource one-period maxima: A 12 mats or 6 baskets; B 4 mats or 4 baskets. Constant opportunity costs, comparable goods, no transport costs. Identify the absolute-advantage producer for each good.
items.canonical_answer: A for mats and A for baskets, using the same resource comparison.
marking_guidance: Feature/example (1): mats A. Distinction/characteristic (1): baskets A.
objective_titles: Describe absolute advantage

items.canonical_answer: Producing at a lower opportunity cost.
objective_titles: Describe comparative advantage

items.prompt: Identify the comparative basket producer from supplied costs: A sacrifices two mats per basket; B sacrifices one. Include the deciding comparison.
items.canonical_answer: B, because one mat is a lower sacrifice than two mats per basket.
marking_guidance: Feature (1): B. Distinction/example (1): lower opportunity cost, 1 versus 2 mats.
objective_titles: Describe comparative advantage

items.prompt: Define comparative advantage (2). Identify exports and imports in this invented country’s transactions: sells mats abroad; buys machines abroad (2). Explain a currency-demand reason for appreciation against a third currency in a hypothetical floating system with unchanged supply (2). Identify the lower-cost basket producer with costs A two mats and B one mat per basket (2).
items.canonical_answer: Comparative advantage is lower opportunity cost. Mats sold abroad are exports; machines bought abroad imports. Stronger foreign demand for the currency can raise its price with supply unchanged in the hypothetical system. B has lower basket cost, one rather than two mats.
marking_guidance: Meaning (2): producing relative to another (1), lower opportunity cost (1). Separate points for flows (2): mats export (1), machines import (1). Explanation (2): stronger currency demand (1), unchanged supply raises price (1). Identification (2): B (1), 1<2 mats sacrifice (1). Marks allocation 8.
objective_titles: Describe comparative advantage

items.prompt: Invented equal-resource one-period maxima: A 12 mats or 6 baskets; B 4 mats or 4 baskets. Constant opportunity costs, comparable goods, no transport costs. Goods values in N$ million for a separate trade example: exports 80 then 100, imports 90 then 120. A Namibia exporter/importer illustration has US$1=N$18 then N$20 with the one-to-one rand peg maintained. A mat exporter has spare capacity and local inputs; an essential-input importer cannot quickly substitute away from dollar purchases. Describe three features: goods balance change, currency movement and comparative basket advantage (6). Explain the comparative-advantage basis for specialisation and the limitation of export growth alone as evidence of external improvement (7). Discuss whether the third-currency movement benefits both illustrative businesses equally (7).
items.canonical_answer: Goods deficit widens N$10m to N$20m; the Namibia dollar depreciates against the dollar under the maintained rand peg; B has basket advantage. A mat costs half a basket versus one for B, while B basket costs one mat versus two. Trade terms between the costs can support mutual gain, but imports grew faster than exports in the separate account. Exporter may benefit with responsive buyers and spare capacity; importer faces dearer essential inputs and limited substitution. Benefits are unequal and trade improvement is conditional.
marking_guidance: Data description (6): deficit widens (1), 10 to 20 detail (1); depreciation (1), N$18 to N$20 third-currency detail (1); B basket advantage (1), 1 versus 2 mat cost (1). Mechanism/explanation (7): A mat cost .5 basket (1), B mat cost 1 (1), B basket cost 1 mat (1), A basket cost 2 (1), between-cost trade permits gain (1); import increase exceeds exports (1), full external account wider than goods (1). Both sides/judgement (7): exporter receipt/price opportunity (1), spare capacity supports response (1); importer input cost rises (1), limited substitution (1); condition buyer response/contracts and peg (1); judgement unequal effects (1), no guaranteed aggregate trade gain (1). Marks allocation 6+7+7=20.

items.prompt: Invented Namibia third-currency depreciation: US$1 rises N$18 to N$20; the one-to-one rand peg is maintained. Case 1: exporter sells dollar-priced output, uses local inputs, has spare capacity and buyers may respond to a competitive offer. Case 2: importer needs US$100 inputs with fixed dollar price and quantity, cannot substitute quickly and cannot pass the full higher cost to customers. Contracts and other costs are unchanged. Evaluate the exporter’s opportunity after this movement (7). Evaluate the importer’s position (7).
items.canonical_answer: Case 1: unchanged dollar receipts convert to more Namibia dollars and spare capacity supports a sales response. Benefit depends on buyer response, contracts and other costs, so it is an opportunity rather than guaranteed profit. Case 2: each US$100 input rises N$1,800 to N$2,000; fixed quantity and limited pass-through squeeze the margin. A later substitute or repricing could help, but immediate disadvantage is supported under the stated maintained-peg third-currency conditions.
marking_guidance: Case 1 marks (7): argument for conversion receipts (1), capacity response (1); argument against uncertain buyer response (1), contracts/costs condition (1); condition maintained peg and responsive market (1); judgement opportunity (1), no guaranteed profit (1). Case 2 allocation (7): argument against N$200 higher input (1), limited pass-through squeezes margin (1); limiting argument later substitutes (1), repricing may change outcome (1); condition fixed current quantity/price and peg (1); judgement immediate disadvantage (1), tied to constrained response (1). Total 14.
